q: In Hormozi's Value Equation, where does he say the best gains usually come from?
a: Cutting the wait and the effort for the buyer
why: Value = (Dream Outcome x Likelihood) / (Time Delay x Effort). Beginners chase bigger claims; the best gains come from making results faster and easier.

q: Hormozi ranks three things by how much they matter. Which comes first?
why: Starving Crowd > Offer Strength > Persuasion Skills. A bad market stops everything.

q: Which of these is NOT one of Hormozi's three ways to grow a business?
w: Get them to buy more times
why: The three ways are more customers, more per purchase, and more purchases. He argues most businesses need to raise prices.

q: What does Hormozi say about scarcity and urgency?
a: They must be real, never fake
w: Only big companies can use them
why: He insists scarcity and urgency be real, "without being phony".

q: "Avoiding stupidity is easier than seeking brilliance" describes which model?
why: Inversion means approaching a problem from the opposite end, for example asking what would guarantee failure.

q: A bounty on cobras led people to breed cobras. Which model does this story teach?
w: The map is not the territory
why: Second-order thinking asks about the effects of the effects. The British cobra bounty in Delhi backfired.

q: "Don't blame on malice what is more easily explained by stupidity" is called...
why: Hanlon's razor: the likeliest explanation has the least intent.

q: What does "the map is not the territory" warn you about?
a: Your model of reality is simplified and can go out of date
why: Models are useful reductions of reality, but imperfect. Reality is the ultimate update.

q: Asking "why?" over and over to reach the real cause is a tool for which model?
why: First principles thinking uses Socratic questioning and the Five Whys to separate facts from assumptions.

q: Naval says you won't get rich renting out your time. What do you need instead?
a: Equity: a piece of a business
why: "You're not going to get rich renting out your time." You must own equity.

q: Which two kinds of leverage does Naval call "permissionless"?
why: Capital and people need someone's permission. Code and media do not, which is why they power the newly rich.

q: According to Naval, if you can't decide, the answer is...
why: "If you can't decide, the answer is no."

q: How does Naval describe specific knowledge?
a: Knowledge you can't be trained for, found by following your curiosity
w: Whatever skill is hot right now
why: Specific knowledge comes from genuine curiosity and passion, not from chasing what's trendy.

q: In Dan Koe's formula, what do you write first?
a: Your anti-vision: the life you refuse to live
w: A list of goals for next year
why: The formula goes anti-vision, then vision, then purpose broken into yearly, monthly, weekly and daily goals.

q: Dan Koe says the most profitable niche is...
why: "The most profitable niche is you": your overlapping skills, interests and experience.

q: What is Levitt's "one important question"?
a: Why should customers come to me instead of where they go now?
w: How much money can I make?
why: Levitt says most new businesses fail because they have no real answer to this question.

q: What does Levitt name as the most common reason new businesses fail?
why: Undercapitalization tops his list, followed by gambling, not delegating and not listening.

q: Levitt says success comes from...
w: Charging as much as you can
why: His Custom Shop sold custom-made shirts for close to the price of ready-made ones.

q: Of Golden's four ways to make money, which does he call the best?
a: Own A System (a business that runs without you)
why: Have A Job and Own A Job are the worst. Sowing money seeds (investing) is second best. Owning a system is best.

q: In Golden's six-can money plan, how much goes to paying bills?
why: The "I can pay my bills" can gets 50%. Three other cans get 10% each: giving, finishing free and educating yourself.

q: Golden says a plumber is not really in the plumbing business. What business is everyone in?
why: Everyone is in the business of marketing what they do.

q: What three things does a simple landing page need?
a: A headline, an image of the free offer, and a sign-up form
w: A video, a price and a timer
A logo, a menu and a blog
Reviews, a chat box and a map
why: An intriguing headline, an image of the lead magnet and an opt-in form. Keep it simple and test.

q: What is a self-liquidating offer for?
a: Front-end sales that pay back the ad cost
why: Price a small offer so its sales cover the ads, which makes the leads break-even or "free".

q: Which lead magnet title follows the book's pain-point formula?
why: "The (#) Biggest Mistakes (audience) Make (when doing X)." Most people move away from pain.

q: What challenge does every expert in Brick & Mortar Funnels answer?
why: Brunson asked 15 local-business experts how they would get 100 customers in the next 100 days.

q: Instead of selling "tax prep", one expert led with what?
a: A free tax assessment that estimates savings
why: Lead with an offer the market wants, not your plain commodity service.

q: What are the 4 U's for scoring a headline?
why: Rate each 1-4. If at least three don't score 3-4, rewrite it.

q: In Bly's motivating sequence, what comes first?
a: Get attention with the strongest benefit
why: Get attention, show a need, satisfy it, prove it, ask for action. Lead with the strongest benefit, not a pun.

q: What do customers really buy?
why: Turn every feature into a reason to buy by asking "so what?"

q: How long does the book say to read each scroll?
why: Read silently when you wake and after the midday meal, and aloud before bed, for 30 days per scroll.

q: Which scroll teaches "I will persist until I succeed"?
why: Scroll III is persistence: each "no" brings you closer to a "yes".

q: Scroll IX is about procrastination. What is its line?
why: Dreams and plans are worthless without action. Repeat "I will act now" until it's a habit.

q: What is David Allen's two-minute rule?
a: If it takes under two minutes, do it right away
w: Spend two minutes planning each day
Take a two-minute break every hour
why: "If an action will take less than two minutes, it should be done at the moment it's defined."

q: In GTD, what makes something a "project"?
a: A result that needs more than one step and can be done within a year
why: A project is any desired result, achievable within a year, that needs more than one action step.

q: What is the "next action" in GTD?
a: The very next physical, visible step
why: Every project gets one next physical action so it can actually move.

q: Greene says every strategy has a...
a: Reversal: a time not to use it
why: Know the limits and counters. Overusing any strategy makes you predictable.

q: Why does Greene favor indirection over direct force?
a: Direct attacks make people resist harder
why: "The ultimate evolution of strategy is toward more and more indirection."
